```{python}
# Opening sqlite3 for a new database.
import sqlite3
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('data/AllCounts_V_4_4.csv')
conn = sqlite3.connect('data/penguins_sights.db')

# Moving data to the DB for the flatfile source
# Priority for this page has been to keep the data managable and and the database quarto applicable
#learning the to work via cursor is the main takeaway with this site
c = conn.cursor()
# basics of the database
x = c.execute("SELECT name, type FROM sqlite_master;")

# checking the objects in the database
objects = x.fetchall()

for name, type in objects:
        print(f"I found a {type} called: {name}")

df.to_sql('observations', conn, if_exists='replace',index=False)
```

The following attributes are available in the below table.
Apparently there no forced not nulls, nor foreign keys present.
A sole table is loaded into the database therefore no relational connections are built.
Easy to target the penguin_count as a fact to be measured in the below visualizations.<br>
The table could be considered ready to any kind of query for the 'business' or analysis.<br>
I intend to run some basic sql queries for desciption and visualizations.

```{python}

# getting the first and last years and the number of observations
# removing 'Anvers' for chart aesthetics
q_sites_obs_range = """SELECT site_id
      ,site_name
      ,min(season_starting) AS "First observation year"
      ,max(season_starting) AS "Last observation year"
      ,max(season_starting) - min(season_starting)+1 AS "Observation range in years"
      ,count(season_starting) AS "Number of observations"
      FROM observations 
      GROUP BY 
      site_id
      ,site_name
      HAVING site_name not like '%Anvers%'
      LIMIT 20;"""
      
df_sites_obs_range= pd.read_sql(q_sites_obs_range, conn)

import plotly.express as px

fig = px.bar(
        df_sites_obs_range,
        x='Observation range in years',
        y='site_name',
        base='First observation year',
        orientation='h',
        color='Number of observations',
        title='Observation Ranges and Counts by Sites',
        labels={"site_name": "Site Name"}
        )
fig.update_layout(
        height=800,
        width=1200,
        coloraxis_colorbar=dict(
                title="Number of Observations",
                thicknessmode="pixels",
                thickness=15,
                orientation="h",
        ),
        xaxis_title='<b>Observation range years</b>',
        yaxis_title='<b>Site name</b>'
)
fig.show()
```

Boxplotting the number of observations to get clarity below.
Clearly saturation of the observations vary greatly which is always a risk for making premature conclusions. <br>
One site is well observed but the most 50 percent of the observations range between 2 and 6.5.
This could point the reader to the fact that most sites are barely observed so do not have solid data to see the population dynamics. <br>
Also there is a spatial and the temporal variation, and I am sure there should be a biologically significant factor of the penguin subspecies as well. <br>
Therefore, this dataset is rather just a raw data to some glimpse into the penguin nests.
This is actually a good point to highlight that oftentimes the job of the data analysis is to clearly set the limitations of the dataset, to avoid false conlusions.

```{python}
# boxplot for number of observations
fig_boxplot = px.box(
        df_sites_obs_range[['Number of observations']],
        points="all",
        y='Number of observations',
        title='Varying number of observations for the sites'
        )

fig_boxplot.update_layout(
        yaxis=dict(
                showgrid=True,
                gridcolor='rgb(200, 200, 200)',
                gridwidth=1,
        ),
        paper_bgcolor='rgb(243, 243, 243)',
        plot_bgcolor='rgb(243, 243, 243)',
        width=800,
)
fig_boxplot.show()
```


The below visualization is will balance the variation slightly.
Only the last observation years are present and for all of the sites.
Therefore we meaningfully observe the population spatially, although not temporally.
Altough qualitative domain knowledge is always a prerequisit for real data analyis.

```{python}
# Selecting the last observation of each site for count visualization
q_last_number_pingi = """WITH last_obs AS (
        SELECT site_id
        ,site_name
        ,longitude_epsg_4326
        ,latitude_epsg_4326
        ,season_starting
       --,printf('%04d-%02d-%02d', year, month,day) AS "DATE"
      ,penguin_count
      ,ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY SITE_ID ORDER BY year DESC, month DESC, day DESC) AS "RN"
      FROM observations)
      SELECT lo.site_id,
      lo.site_name,
      lo.season_starting,
      lo.longitude_epsg_4326,
      lo.latitude_epsg_4326,
      lo.penguin_count 
      FROM last_obs lo 
      WHERE lo.RN = 1;"""

df_last_number_pingi = pd.read_sql(q_last_number_pingi, conn)

# changing numbers to whole number
df_last_number_pingi['penguin_count']= df_last_number_pingi['penguin_count'].astype('Int64')

df_last_number_pingi = df_last_number_pingi.astype({
        'site_id': 'category',
        'site_name': 'category',
        'season_starting': 'category'
})

import pydeck as pdk

layer = pdk.Layer(
        "HexagonLayer",
        data= df_last_number_pingi,
        get_position=["longitude_epsg_4326","latitude_epsg_4326"],
        auto_highlight=True,
        elevation_scale=50,
        pickable=True,
        elevation_range=[0, 3000],
        extruded=True,
        coverage=1
)

view_state= pdk.ViewState(
        latitude= -64.737905,
        longitude= -63.896758,
        zoom=3.5,
        pitch=45,
        bearing=0
)
#Render 
r = pdk.Deck(layers=[layer], initial_view_state=view_state)
r.to_html("hexagon_map.html")
```
